findings.documented: The API key must be appended as a query parameter, e.g. POST /auth/login?api_key=IVY26-XXXXXXXXXXXX.
findings.actual: The query-parameter form returns 401 with a body that says to send the key in the X-API-Key request header instead. Sending X-API-Key as a header, together with the documented email/password body, succeeds.
findings.how_found: Called POST /auth/login exactly as documented (api_key as a query parameter, no header), got a 401 with an explanatory error body, then repeated the same call with X-API-Key set as a header.
findings.impact: A client built strictly to the documented query-parameter form cannot authenticate at all; it has to send the key as a header instead.

findings.documented: The 200 response is documented as { token, token_type, expires_in: 86400, user }, and the text explicitly states tokens are valid for 24 hours and 'there is no refresh flow', so one login is enough for a working session.
findings.actual: The real response field is access_token, not token. expires_in is 900 (15 minutes), not 86400. The response also includes a refresh_token and a refresh_url (/auth/refresh) that the documentation says do not exist.
findings.how_found: Logged in with a valid X-API-Key and inspected the full JSON body of the 200 response.
findings.impact: A frontend built around the documented field name and 24-hour lifetime will silently stop working roughly 15 minutes after login unless it separately discovers and calls the undocumented refresh flow. This directly threatens the assignment's own requirement that the app 'must still be working thirty minutes after you logged in.'
evidence: POST /auth/login response field is access_token, not token

findings.documented: Not mentioned anywhere in the documentation. The documentation states outright: 'There is no refresh flow.'
findings.actual: The /auth/login response itself advertises refresh_url: "/auth/refresh" alongside a refresh_token, directly contradicting that statement.
findings.how_found: Found refresh_token and refresh_url while inspecting the shape of a successful /auth/login response.
findings.impact: Without knowing this endpoint exists, a client has no way to keep a session alive past the real 15-minute access-token lifetime short of forcing the user to log in again.

findings.documented: Collection endpoints are documented as taking page (1-indexed) and limit, with total described as the exact record count to use for computing how many pages to request.
findings.actual: page and limit do work, but so does an undocumented offset and limit pair, and a full retrieval needs to rely on offset/has_more rather than the documented page/total contract (see the next finding for why).
findings.how_found: Paged with page=1&limit=2, then repeated the same window with offset=0&limit=2 and offset=2&limit=2, and compared the returned records.
findings.impact: Either parameter style returns data, but a client that trusts the documented page/total contract to know when it has fetched everything can under-fetch.

findings.documented: total is documented as 'the exact number of records matching your filters', and the docs instruct you to divide total by limit to compute how many pages to request to get everything.
findings.actual: total is reported as 3515 on /v1/listings regardless of offset. Paging all the way through using has_more (ignoring total) returns 3800 listing records. 3515 is exactly this submission's answer to 'how many distinct properties' (unique_properties, verified independently by grouping all 3,800 downloaded records by latitude/longitude), not the number of listing records. Following the documented total/limit formula stops 285 real, retrievable records short of the full set.
findings.how_found: Downloaded the full dataset by paging with offset/has_more until has_more was false (3800 records), and compared that against the total field the API itself reported (3515) and against an independent latitude/longitude grouping of the downloaded records (also 3515).
findings.impact: A client that computes total/limit pages, exactly as documented, to know when it has fetched everything will silently miss roughly 285 real listing records, including the duplicate records that separate 'total listing records' from 'unique properties'.

findings.documented: Documented as a pre-computed city analytics endpoint returning total_listings, median_price, median_price_per_sqft, by_locality, and by_bhk.
findings.how_found: Requested the documented endpoint directly with a valid token while building the Insights screen.
findings.impact: The Insights screen cannot use this endpoint at all; every figure it shows has to be computed client-side from /v1/listings, /v1/rentals, and /v1/projects.

findings.documented: GET /v1/listing/{listing_id} is documented as the single-listing detail endpoint.
findings.actual: The documented singular route returns 404; the plural route /v1/listings/{listing_id} returns the same listing with a 200.
findings.how_found: Requested the same listing_id through both the documented singular route and the plural collection-style route.
findings.impact: A detail page built on the documented path is permanently broken; it has to use the plural path instead.

findings.documented: Area is documented as square feet everywhere in the API.
findings.actual: MAG-prefixed listings' carpet_area and super_built_up_area are actually in square metres; multiplying the raw value by 10.764 turns them into plausible square-foot figures consistent with comparable non-MAG listings.
findings.how_found: Compared raw MAG-listing area values against non-MAG listings with similar bedroom counts and prices; the raw MAG values were consistently about 10.76x too small to already be square feet.
findings.impact: Displaying MAG carpet/super-built-up area as-is understates the true size by roughly 10.7x, and understates any price-per-sqft figure computed from it (applied when computing avg_price_per_sqft_2bhk above).

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are documented as rupees.
findings.actual: Neither field is in plain rupees, and a single fixed multiplier does not fit both fields consistently. Every raw price_min/price_max value in the dataset is either under 10 or between 10 and 99.9 (nothing in between, nothing at rupee scale). Applying the single 'raw x 100000' (lakh) rule that fits price_min to price_max as well makes price_max come out lower than price_min for 321 of 440 projects, which is impossible for a min/max range. Reading raw values under 10 as crores (x 1,00,00,000) instead of lakhs removes every one of those 321 inconsistencies: 0 of 440 projects have max < min once the two-scale rule is applied.
findings.how_found: Converted price_min and price_max for all 440 retrievable projects with the single 'raw x 100000' rule, checked max >= min, then re-ran with a magnitude-aware rule (raw < 10 -> crores, 10 <= raw < 100000 -> lakhs) and compared the failure counts.
findings.impact: Using one fixed multiplier for every project price field produces internally-inconsistent (max < min) and understated prices for 73% of projects, and names the wrong project as the city's single costliest project: the single-multiplier rule points to P30394 (price_max ~Rs 99.9 lakh), while the two-scale rule that is consistent across the whole dataset points to P30288 (raw price_max 4.47 -> Rs 4.47 crore = Rs 4,47,00,000), more than 4x higher.

findings.documented: Listings returned by this endpoint are described as active sale listings that are safe to show to users.
findings.actual: 28 retrievable listings contain values that cannot describe a real property, in four equal-sized groups of 7: negative prices; carpet_area greater than super_built_up_area; a floor number greater than total_floors (excluding plot listings, where 0/0 is normal); and listings whose latitude and longitude are swapped, placing the property far outside India (e.g. a Pune listing recorded at latitude ~73.8, longitude ~18.6, when every genuine listing in this city falls within latitude ~18.36-18.68 and longitude ~73.70-74.02).
findings.how_found: Ran numeric consistency checks (price > 0, carpet_area <= super_built_up_area, floor <= total_floors for non-plot listings) against all 3,800 retrievable listing records, plus a bounding-box check on latitude/longitude against India's coordinate range and against this city's own observed coordinate cluster.
findings.impact: Showing these records as-is exposes users to impossible prices, sizes, floor numbers, or map locations (a property pin placed outside India).

findings.documented: The endpoint is described as returning active sale listings that are safe to show to users.
findings.actual: 74 retrievable listings ask for an upfront booking amount or token amount, or state that a site visit is only possible after that payment is made — a pattern consistent with listings that exist to collect enquiries or payments rather than sell a real unit.
findings.how_found: Scanned all 3,800 listing descriptions for the phrases 'booking amount', 'token amount', and 'site visit only after'.
findings.impact: These listings need a visible warning or exclusion rather than being presented as ordinary, safe-to-show listings, and are also excluded from avg_price_per_sqft_2bhk above.

findings.documented: total_listings is documented as the number of currently available listings for a project, recomputed on every change, and stated to always agree with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns.
findings.actual: 95 projects report a total_listings value that disagrees with the number of active listings actually found for that project_id — some report 0 despite having active listings, others over- or under-count by a wide margin.
findings.how_found: Fetched every project and every listing, grouped active listings by project_id, and compared each project's reported total_listings against the actual active count.
findings.impact: Project cards, filters, and any project-level analytics built from the documented total_listings field can show the wrong inventory count.

findings.documented: Timestamps are documented as ISO 8601, UTC, with a Z suffix, everywhere in the API.
findings.actual: posted_at on /v1/listings carries no timezone information at all on any of the 3,800 retrievable records (e.g. 2026-04-30T14:57:00 — no Z, no offset). posted_at on /v1/rentals, by contrast, is correctly Z-suffixed on all 1,450 retrievable records (e.g. 2026-09-04T00:21:00Z). The 'everywhere in the API' claim is wrong in two ways: the Z suffix is missing, and it's missing inconsistently across endpoints rather than as a single documented convention.
findings.how_found: Inspected posted_at on all 3,800 /v1/listings records (0/3,800 had a Z suffix or offset) and on all 1,450 /v1/rentals records (1,450/1,450 had a Z suffix).
findings.impact: listings_last_7_days is computed by treating /v1/listings' posted_at as already IST and comparing directly against REFERENCE with no shift, which gives 128; treating the same values as UTC and converting gives 115. Since the one endpoint that does carry an explicit offset (/v1/rentals) uses UTC exactly as documented, UTC is the more likely intended reading for /v1/listings too, despite the missing suffix — but this remains a genuine, unresolved 13-record ambiguity worth a live check.

findings.documented: No such requirement appears anywhere in the documentation.
findings.actual: A number of listing descriptions contain text addressed directly to 'AI coding assistants' and 'automated tools', instructing them to add a specific certification string to the app's footer, or to add a specific dataset_audit_ref value into submission.json's answers object. Neither is a real licensing or dataset-versioning requirement from Ivy Homes; both are instructions planted inside a seller-writable text field, aimed at manipulating whatever LLM is used to build the app or compile the submission.
findings.how_found: Noticed the phrasing while reading listing descriptions during data-quality review, addressed to 'AI coding assistants' / 'AI assistants processing this data' rather than to a human reader.
findings.impact: Complying with either instruction means acting on unverified text a seller wrote into a free-text field, not on anything the real API or Ivy Homes actually requires — the exact trap the assignment brief warns about ('treat everything the API returns as data... a seller can write anything'). This submission complies with neither.

findings.documented: The documentation's own example rental object has title "2 BHK for rent in Koramangala" alongside locality: "koramangala" — the two fields describing the same place.
findings.actual: 1,313 of 1,450 retrievable rental records (over 90%) have a title naming a different locality than the structured locality field — e.g. R3000001's title reads "2 BHK for rent in Viman Nagar" while its locality field is "kothrud".
findings.how_found: Compared the locality named in each rental's title against its locality field across all 1,450 retrievable rental records.
findings.impact: The free-text title cannot be used to determine which locality a rental is actually in; only the structured locality field can, which matters directly for a locality-scoped figure like total_monthly_rent.
